newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Protesting pilot lands at wrong Cyprus airport.
newsitem.headline: Protesting pilot lands at wrong Cyprus airport.

text.p: New financing for Cyprus Airways is in jeopardy because a pilot refused to work 10 minutes overtime and landed at the wrong airport, the Cypriot government said Wednesday.
On Monday, a flight carrying 153 passengers landed in the western resort of Paphos instead of Larnaca on the southern coast after a technical hitch delayed departure from Zurich for two hours.

According to the airline, the plane would have needed five to six minutes to fly the 150 km (90 miles) between Paphos and Larnaca. Instead, buses and taxis were used to ferry the passengers to a resort at the other end of the island, while the pilot spent the night in a luxury hotel.

"This was foolish, irresponsible and arrogant behaviour which in the final analysis undermines the company itself and undermines the Cypriot economy," Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou told reporters.
The pilots union PASIPI is enforcing work-to-rule measures to protest the transfer of some work from Cyprus Airways to Eurocypria, its charter subsidiary.

"There has been an application from Cyprus Airways for a new loan guaranteed by the government of tens of millions of pounds. It will not be handled favourably if this will continue to be the behaviour of those guiding employees in Cyprus Airways," Christodoulou warned.
Monday's incident was just the latest in a long string of labour disputes plaguing the national carrier, which is 80-percent state owned. Twenty percent is traded on the Cyprus stock exchange.
Last month caterers banned from watching television by management caused a 45 minute delay to an outbound Gulf Air flight. They went on strike for an hour when they found their TV set was missing.

Last week the Cyprus Airways group announced a preliminary consolidated pre-tax loss of 2.15 million pounds ($4.2 million) in 1996, compared with a pre-tax profit of 5.03 million pounds in 1995. The company has blamed falling load factors and increased fuel prices for the decline.
